title: How to Think Like a System Designer
subtitle: From bouncers to databases: the plan behind apps that serve millions
intro: Your save lists 25 system design questions — from Rate Limiter to YouTube — all asking the same thing: how would you build this for millions?
takeaway: System design is planning how parts scale and fail together before you write code.

sections.heading: Analogy: designing a city before building it
sections.body:
Imagine you run a busy restaurant. You need a bouncer at the door, a fast kitchen, and labeled shelves.

System design is that plan for apps. A Rate Limiter is the bouncer, a Distributed Key-Value Store — a database spread across many machines — is the shelves.

You draw this plan before coding, which is why it matters next.

sections.heading: Why it exists: handling millions without breaking
sections.body:
You need this because one computer cannot serve millions. Your save lists 25 interview designs like URL Shortener, YouTube Video Streaming, and WhatsApp Chat.

Each handles scale differently. A News Feed must rank posts for millions, Streaming must send huge video without buffering.

Without this plan your app crashes under load, and even with it things can still go wrong.

sections.heading: What can go wrong: when good plans fail
sections.body:
Even good designs break. If your Rate Limiter is too strict, real users get blocked; too loose and bots flood you.

If your Key-Value Store loses sync, one Instagram user sees an old photo while another sees the new one. Notification queues can overflow and delay chats.

So you must trade speed, freshness, and cost before you build.

steps.narration: Millions of users hit your app at once.
Rate Limiter decides who gets in now.
App builds Feed, Chat, or Video response.
Distributed Store fetches data from many machines.
Queue sends notifications without blocking users.

quiz.q: What does a Rate Limiter do in system design?
options: Controls how many requests get in
quiz.why: Like a bouncer, it protects the system from being flooded.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x without good design?
options: One server overloads and requests queue or crash
quiz.why: One machine cannot handle millions; queues overflow and sync breaks.

quiz.q: Why is a Distributed Key-Value Store spread across many machines?
options: To make the app look pretty
To store more and stay available if one machine fails
quiz.why: Distribution gives scale and resilience, but can cause temporary inconsistency.
